{{One Name Study|name=Glasgow}}

== Introduction ==

The Glasgow Name Study brings together documentary, genealogical and Y-DNA research concerning the '''Glasgow''' surname and its historical variants.

The story begins with medieval people styled ''de Glasgu''—“of” or “from Glasgow”—and follows the name as it moved through merchant, church, royal and burgh society. By the later fifteenth century, forms such as '''Glasgow''' and '''Glasgw''' were being used without ''de''. During the sixteenth century, the surviving town-clerk protocols begin to reveal spouses, children, inherited property, occupations and civic responsibilities, allowing the first secure multi-generation Glasgow pedigrees to be reconstructed.

Later records place Glasgow households in Ayrshire, Renfrewshire, Lothian, the Borders and Ulster before the surname spread more widely through migration.

This page provides the main chronological overview. Detailed bearer registers, source extracts, profile audits, branch reconstructions and DNA analysis are kept on linked research pages so that the distinction between documented evidence and working hypotheses remains clear.

<span id='ancient_paternal_origins'></span>
== Ancient paternal origins ==

{{Image|file=Glasgow_Ancient_YDNA-3.png
|size=L
|caption=Estimated deep paternal migration pathway for the principal Glasgow Y-DNA cluster. Generated using [http://scaledinnovation.com/gg/snpTracker.html SNP Tracker]
}}

The principal tested Glasgow paternal line belongs to the wider '''R-M269 > R-U106 > R-Z18 > R-Z17''' family of Y-DNA branches.

These branches predate hereditary surnames by thousands of years. They place the deeper paternal ancestry within the broad northern European and North Sea genetic world, but they cannot identify a medieval Scottish ancestor or explain when the Glasgow surname was adopted.

All men currently assigned to the project’s principal Glasgow surname cluster descend through '''[[Space:R-FT25406|R-FT25406]]'''. The present genetic estimate gives a '''most likely common ancestor around 1429 CE''', displayed by the testing platform as approximately '''1450 CE'''. The full 95% probability range is much broader—'''1195 to 1607 CE'''—and may change as more men test and the calculation method is refined.<ref name="GlasgowDNAProject">[https://www.familytreedna.com/public/Glasgow?iframe=ysnp FamilyTreeDNA Glasgow Surname DNA Project, public Y-DNA SNP results], accessed 31 July 2026; see also [[Space:Glasgow DNA|Glasgow DNA]].</ref><ref name="FT25406Estimate">FamilyTreeDNA Discover estimate for R-FT25406: most likely 1429 CE, displayed as 1450 CE, with a 95% interval of 1195–1607 CE. See [[Space:R-FT25406|R-FT25406]].</ref>

The estimate is genetic rather than genealogical. It does not identify the common ancestor as the Glasgow burgess of 1447, the Stirling witness of the 1470s or any other named bearer.

Its importance is narrower: the most likely date falls near the period when the documentary record begins to show Glasgow behaving as a settled surname. Testing may eventually help determine which documented paternal lines share that surname-era ancestor, but only where each tester also has a supported documentary pedigree.

For the full genetic research, see:

* [[Space:Glasgow Ancient YDNA|Glasgow ancient Y-DNA]]
* [[Space:Glasgow DNA|Glasgow surname DNA project]]
* [[Space:R-FT25406|R-FT25406]]
* [https://groups.io/g/glasgowdnaproject Glasgow DNA Project discussion group]

<span id='current_conclusion'></span>
== Current conclusion ==

<blockquote>
Personal use of ''de Glasgu'' is documented from the late twelfth century. Repeated and unprefixed surname forms are visible by the later fifteenth century, and the surname remains in documentary use into the sixteenth-century Glasgow burgh records. The first secure multi-generation burgh pedigree begins with William Glasgow and Esbell Brade in the 1530s. A direct descent from the medieval bearers to that family—and a single pedigree joining every later Scottish and Ulster branch—has not yet been proved.
</blockquote>

The evidence therefore reaches several different levels:

# '''personal locative or byname use''' — documented from the late twelfth century;
# '''repeated surname-like use by the same individual''' — documented before 1400;
# '''fixed or unprefixed surname forms''' — clear by the later fifteenth century;
# '''explicit parent-child relationships under the surname''' — documented securely in the sixteenth-century burgh and regional records;
# '''one continuous pedigree joining all bearers''' — not proved.

The surname record is substantially continuous. The complete genealogy is not.

<span id='surname_story'></span>
== The story of the surname ==

=== 1. The medieval name: ''de Glasgu'', c.1175–1506 ===

The earliest known personal bearers appear in the late twelfth century. By 1300, the surviving evidence contains twelve working identities using forms such as ''de Glasgu'', ''de Glascu'', ''de Glasgw'' and ''de Glasgow''.

Roger de Glasgu witnessed a Glasgow burgh and Clyde fishery grant. Richard and Robert de Glasgu were admitted consecutively to the Dublin guild merchant, while Gilbert de Glascu appears later in the same roll. In 1238/39, Alexander was admitted as the son of Robert de Glascu, providing the earliest known father-son construction associated with the name.

Other early bearers include Robert de Glascu in an English royal plea roll in 1200; Robert de Glasgu in the household of the bishop of Dunkeld; another Robert in a Durham episcopal witness group; and Alexander de Glasgu or de Glasgow, royal escheator south of the Forth in 1289/90.

'''[[Space:John de Glasgu|John de Glasgu]]''' is securely recorded as chaplain to Bishop Gamelin of St Andrews on 2 February 1259.<ref name="RPSA173">''Registrum Prioratus Sancti Andree'' (Bannatyne Club, 1841), p. 173.</ref> He was probably also the John de Glasgu who witnessed a Cambuskenneth Abbey charter concerning Dunipace because both records include Richard de Stickley. A separate John of Glasgow appears among the Holyrood community in 1299, but no surviving evidence proves that he was the same man.

The strongest pre-1300 surname-like occurrence within Glasgow itself is '''Hugh de Glasgw''', who witnessed a Rottenrow property transaction around 1283. The deed already identifies Glasgow as the location and civic authority, yet Hugh is still individually distinguished as ''Hugone de Glasgw''. The name was therefore performing personal identifying work rather than merely stating the venue.

The surrounding Paisley-register acts define two associated property holders who must not be collapsed into a surname pedigree: '''[[Space:Alexander_son_of_Richard_messenger_of_Glasgow|Alexander, son of the late Richard the messenger of Glasgow]]''' and '''[[Space:Alexander_son_of_Richard_constable_of_Glasgow|Alexander, son of Richard the former constable of Glasgow]]'''. Their father–son relationships are explicit, but the Glasgow wording may describe each father's office or location rather than an inherited surname. Richard the messenger's son is a plausible local candidate for the 1289/90 escheator, not an established identity.

Repeated use becomes clearer during the fourteenth century.

William de Glascou appears as vicar of Corbridge in records of 1315 and 1322. '''Master John de Glasgow''' appears in at least five explicit contemporary records before 1400, including records naming him as chancellor of Dunkeld and probably as canon of Aberdeen. In these documents, ''de Glasgow'' forms part of his personal designation and is grammatically separate from his ecclesiastical offices.

A Scottish Exchequer account of 1394 names Malcolm, son of John de Glasgu, providing a second explicit father-son construction. William, physician de Glasgu, was then recorded twice in royal accounts in 1395 and 1397.

The records show the name in several social settings:

* Dublin merchants;
* royal and episcopal officials;
* priests, canons and monks;
* Glasgow civic and property witnesses;
* a physician;
* a Berwick burgess and landholder;
* and people moving through the institutional networks of Glasgow, Dunkeld, Durham, Melrose, Holyrood and Arbroath.

This variety matters. ''De Glasgu'' was not simply an adjective applied to bishops, churches or dioceses. It functioned as a personal locative, stable byname and surname-form.

Pre-1400 surname use can therefore be demonstrated in the functional medieval sense of a repeated identifying second name. What remains unproved is hereditary transmission: the father-son constructions identify Robert and John as Glasgow-designated fathers, but do not show their sons using Glasgow as an inherited surname. Descent is a separate question and may be proved even when a child uses another byname; conversely, shared Glasgow names and compatible dates do not prove descent. One reliable instrument explicitly naming a Glasgow-designated father and son could demonstrate transmission in that act without an artificial two-document requirement, though wider identities would still need corroboration.

By the later fifteenth century, the transition towards fixed forms is clearer. A John Glasgw appears twice at Stirling without ''de'', while Alan Glasgw is named in a Border criminal proceeding in 1495. In 1506, John de Glasgow alias Smith was active in a Glasgow property transaction, showing that Glasgow could coexist with an explicit alternative name.

These men cannot yet be joined genealogically to one another or to the sixteenth-century burgh families.

The complete bearer register, source criticism, disputed readings and identity problems are collected at:

'''[https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Space:Bearers_of_the_%27%27de_Glasgu%27%27_Name_and_the_Emergence_of_the_Glasgow_Surname%2C_c.1175%E2%80%931500 Bearers of the ''de Glasgu'' Name and the Emergence of the Glasgow Surname]'''

=== 2. From fixed surname forms to early Scottish families, c.1447–1650 ===

From the mid-fifteenth century, the records begin to show more than isolated personal bynames. They show repeated surname forms, urban property, occupations, spouses, children, inheritance and participation in the government and economy of the burgh.

The change was gradual. It should not be represented as one medieval bearer suddenly becoming the ancestor of every later Glasgow family.

Four stages are visible:

{| class="wikitable"
! Period
! Development
! Evidential position
|-
| '''1447–1506'''
| Repeated fixed or unprefixed surname forms in Glasgow, Stirling and the Borders
| Surname continuity proved; relationships between bearers unproved
|-
| '''1526–1534'''
| William Glasgow enters royal and Glasgow burgh records; William and Esbell Brade transfer property to their son John
| First secure bridge into the documented burgh pedigree
|-
| '''1550s–1590s'''
| Glasgow households appear as fishers, citizens, landholders, witnesses, curators and municipal officers
| A compact civic network is visible, but not every household is genealogically joined
|-
| '''1559–1650'''
| Independent or partly connected clusters appear in Ayrshire, Lothian and the Borders
| Regional spread proved; routes of descent remain mixed
|}

==== Late-medieval continuity ====

A '''[[Space:John Glasgow-1|John de Glasgu]]''' was recorded as a Glasgow burgess and property witness in 1447 and 1455.<ref name="John1447">''Liber Collegii Nostre Domine: Munimenta Fratrum Predicatorum de Glasgu'' (Glasgow, 1846), acts dated 21 June 1447 and 10 April 1455.</ref>

A '''John Glasgw''' later witnessed Stirling property and religious-endowment acts in 1475 and 1479/80.<ref name="StirlingJohn">''Charters and Other Documents Relating to the Royal Burgh of Stirling, A.D. 1124–1705'' (Glasgow, 1884), charters dated 11 April 1475 and 2 March 1479/80.</ref>

The chronology permits several interpretations:

* the Glasgow and Stirling records concern one mobile man;
* the Stirling witness belonged to the next generation;
* the two men were collateral relatives;
* or they represented separate families already using the settled surname.

No shared property, office, seal, notary, repeated witness or explicit family relationship currently identifies them as one person.

The Stirling records nevertheless form an important part of the story. They show the unprefixed form '''Glasgw''' being used repeatedly in another royal burgh before 1480. The surname did not disappear between the medieval ''de Glasgu'' records and the sixteenth-century Glasgow protocols.

The sequence continues with:

* '''[[Glasgow-3023|Alan Glasgow]]''', named in a Border justice proceeding by 26 February 1495;<ref name="Alan1495">Robert Pitcairn, ed., ''Criminal Trials in Scotland'', vol. I, part I (Edinburgh, 1833), p. 19, Jedburgh justice ayre, 26 February 1495.</ref>
* '''[[Space:John Glasgow|John de Glasgow alias Smith]]''', joint acquirer of a four-shilling annual rent from Glasgow High Street property in 1506. The seller was Agnes, daughter and heir of Robert Watson; the catalogue does not state John's occupation or a relationship to co-acquirer Sir Allan Smith.<ref name="AliasSmith1506">Glasgow University Archives, Blackhouse Charters, GUA BL/204, formerly GUA 16403, instrument dated 28 April 1506; [https://yourscottisharchives.com/catalogues/565b7ef3-fc87-3f6f-aaac-149925faa39d?component-id=7cdbf375-dc6d-3de3-b53a-86376e2106da Your Scottish Archives catalogue description]. The complete instrument has not been inspected.</ref>

These records demonstrate continuing surname use. None names an heir or supplies a direct relationship to the later burgh family.

The remaining break is therefore genealogical rather than documentary.

==== The first proved burgh pedigree ====

A William Glasgow appears in a royal remission dated 2 July 1526, among men remitted for the slaughter of James Somervile and other offences.<ref name="William1526">''Registrum Secreti Sigilli Regum Scotorum'', vol. I, no. 3433, remission dated 2 July 1526.</ref>

The chronology and central-Scotland associations are compatible with '''[[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]]''', but the remission gives no wife, parent, occupation, property or explicit residence. It is a possible earlier occurrence rather than conclusive identification.

William’s secure Glasgow civic career begins in the surviving town-clerk protocols.

On 28 February 1530/31, he witnessed a property transaction on Our Lady’s Street. He appeared alongside a tailor, another citizen and a burgh sergeant, within the ordinary legal machinery through which sasines and property transfers were recorded.<ref name="William1531">Robert Renwick, ed., ''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', protocol no. 1058, 28 February 1530/31.</ref>

The decisive record followed on 31 December 1534.

William Glasgow, with the consent of his wife '''[[Brade-232|Esbell Brade]]''', resigned a back tenement to:

* '''[[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]]''', described as their son;
* and '''[[Spreull-4|Jonet Spreull]]''', John’s wife.

William and Esbell reserved the profits during their lifetimes.<ref name="WilliamJohn1534">''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', protocol dated 31 December 1534 at 10 a.m., recording the resignation by William Glasgow and Esbell Brade to their son John Glasgow and his wife Jonet Spreull.</ref>

This is the first secure parent-child link in the later Glasgow burgh family:

: [[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]] and [[Brade-232|Esbell Brade]]
:: → [[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]] and [[Spreull-4|Jonet Spreull]]

William was dead by about 1543, when adjoining property was described by reference to the lands of the late William Glasgow.

No inspected record identifies him as the son, heir or relative of the Glasgow burgess of 1447–1455, the Stirling witness, Alan Glasgw or John alias Smith.

==== A family inside the sixteenth-century burgh ====

The later records begin to place the family physically within Glasgow’s streets, property boundaries and civic institutions.

John Glasgow and Jonet Spreull received property from John’s parents in 1534. A protocol dated 24 August 1565 records John Glasgow senior resigning a burgage tenement to:

<blockquote>
'''William Glesgw, his son'''
</blockquote>

John reserved liferent to himself and Jonet Spreull, his spouse.<ref name="JohnWilliam1565">Robert Renwick, ed., ''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', vol. III, protocol no. 847, p. 73, 24 August 1565.</ref>

This proves '''[[Glasgow-3522|William Glasgow]]''' as John’s son. Jonet is named as John’s spouse and joint liferenter, although the surviving abstract does not expressly call the younger William her son.

A record dated 8 November 1575 identifies '''[[Glasgow-1029|Stephen Glasgow]]''' as the son of the late John Glasgow and names Jonet Spreull as his mother.<ref name="Stephen1575">Glasgow protocol abstract dated 8 November 1575, identifying Stephen Glasgow as son of the late John Glasgow and naming Jonet Spreull as his mother. The complete volume, protocol number and printed page remain to be added after direct verification.</ref>

The secure core therefore becomes:

: [[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]] and [[Brade-232|Esbell Brade]]
:: → [[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]] and [[Spreull-4|Jonet Spreull]]
::: → [[Glasgow-1029|Stephen Glasgow]]
::: → [[Glasgow-3522|William Glasgow]]

This was not a family visible only in births and deaths. Its members appear in property transfers, boundary descriptions, sasines, curatorships and municipal appointments.

Stephen Glasgow was a landholder and repeated participant in the protocol books. His property lay within the urban landscape running between the cathedral, Market Cross, South Port and nearby crofts. He witnessed sasines, sold and acquired tenements, appeared in boundary proceedings and acted as curator to a younger Glasgow heir.

He also served as '''water bailie''', an office concerned with the river, harbour activity and the enforcement of burgh regulations. The precise year or repeated years of his service still require reconciliation between the surviving references, but the office itself places him within Glasgow’s municipal government.

Stephen was not a town clerk. His connection to the town-clerk network is broader: the burgh’s clerks and notaries repeatedly recorded his land, relatives, legal responsibilities and public office.

His brother or half-brother William married '''[[Herbison-439|Margaret Herbesoun]]'''. William was dead by July 1586, when their son '''[[Glasgow-1099|George Glasgow]]''' received sasine as his heir.

George was still under legal curatorship. In September 1586 he acted with the consent of:

* Margaret Herbesoun, his mother and liferenter;
* Sir William Herbesoun;
* and Stephen Glasgow, his curator.

<ref name="George1586">''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', protocols dated 15 July and 1 September 1586, recording George Glasgow as heir to the late William Glasgow and naming Margaret Herbesoun, Sir William Herbesoun and Stephen Glasgow.</ref>

Stephen’s curatorship is particularly useful evidence. It places him in a legally recognised position of trust within the next generation and supports the reconstruction of a real family network rather than one built only from shared surnames.

==== Fishers, burgesses and neighbouring households ====

Other Glasgow households were active in the same civic world.

'''[[Glasgow-1096|Robert Glasgow]]''' appears as a fisher, citizen and property holder. He and his wife '''[[Rolland-239|Margaret Rolland]]''' transferred property near the Market Cross and South Port. Their tenement bordered land belonging to another John Glasgow.

The shared surname, occupation, neighbouring holdings and repeated appearances suggest close association. They do not by themselves establish whether Robert and John were brothers, cousins or members of separate households.

A burgess admission dated 23 October 1596 describes '''[[Glasgow-3188|Ninian Glasgow]]''' as:

<blockquote>
'''second son to Robert G., fisher, burgess'''
</blockquote>

<ref name="Ninian1596">James R. Anderson, ed., ''Burgesses & Guild Brethren of Glasgow, 1573–1750'' (Scottish Record Society, 1925), p. 24, entry dated 23 October 1596.</ref>

Ninian’s testament, made in January 1613, names brother John, sister
[[Glasgow-3062|Marion]], spouse [[Hutcheson-1774|Jonet Hutchesoun]] and son
Robert. William occurs, but the previously asserted sonship wording is not
secure in the supplied working transcription.<ref name="Ninian1613">National Records of Scotland, Glasgow Commissary Court, CC9/7/9, images 142–145, testament of Niniane Glasgw, fisher and burgess of Glasgow, made 10 January 1613.</ref>

The records directly establish:

: Robert Glasgow, fisher and burgess
:: → John Glasgow, whose birth order is not stated
:: → [[Glasgow-3188|Ninian Glasgow]], second son

The documented [[Glasgow-1096|Robert Glasgow]] is Ninian's record-supported
father. Margaret Rolland is a maternal candidate, but no reviewed record calls
her Ninian's mother.

Ninian’s family reflects the economic character of the burgh. He was a fisher and burgess, operating within the Clyde’s fishing, transport and maritime world. His household appears in burgess and testamentary records rather than in noble pedigrees or national land grants.

Elsewhere in the burgh, '''[[Glasgow-1097|Archibald Glasgow]]''' and '''[[Newlands-647|Isobell Newlands]]''' acquired property near the South Port in 1551. A Robert Glasgow witnessed the transaction. The record proves the couple and their property, but not Archibald’s parents, Robert’s relationship to him or the children currently attached on WikiTree.

The picture is therefore of several surname households repeatedly crossing the same urban records:

* fishers and river workers;
* citizens and burgesses;
* property holders and neighbouring tenants;
* witnesses and procurators;
* civic officers and curators;
* and families linked through marriage, credit and inheritance.

Their social world was compact. Close kinship between some households is likely, but the exact relationships cannot be reconstructed merely from the small population of the burgh or the rarity of the surname.

==== Parallel regional clusters ====

The sixteenth-century evidence also establishes Glasgow families outside the burgh.

In the Cunninghame teind material of 1559–60, James Glasgow elder and James Glasgow younger were listed at Corsinkell in Stevenston parish.<ref name="CorsinkellTeinds">Margaret H. B. Sanderson, “The People of Sixteenth Century Ayrshire”, ''Ayrshire Collections'', vol. XIV, appendix “The Cunninghame Teind Lists of 1559–60”, p. 331.</ref>

On 9 February 1571, Corsinkell was described as occupied by James Glasgow elder and by '''James and John Glasgow, his sons'''.<ref name="Corsinkell1571">National Records of Scotland, Charter Chest of the Earls of Glencairn, GD39/5/59, letters of reversion concerning the 40-shilling land of Corsinkell, 9 February 1571.</ref>

This proves an Ayrshire father-son group:

: [[Glasgow-1168|James Glasgow elder]]
:: → [[Glasgow-3921|James Glasgow younger]]
:: → a son John Glasgow

No inspected source identifies James elder as a son of William Glasgow and Esbell Brade. The Corsinkell family should therefore be treated as a documented parallel cluster rather than automatically inserted into the Glasgow burgh pedigree.

A separate '''[[Glasgow-3181|John Glasgow in Hirmanscheillis]]''' died in November 1576, leaving a widow, Margaret Hoghame, and daughters Katherine and Marjorie.<ref name="Hirmanscheillis1576">National Records of Scotland, Edinburgh Commissary Court, CC8/8/5, image 276 and the upper portion of image 277, testament dative and inventory of Johne Glasgw in Hirmanscheillis.</ref>

This John cannot be the brother named in Ninian Glasgow’s 1613 testament because Ninian’s brother was then alive.

The Hirmanscheillis household is therefore another independently documented family which must not be merged into the burgh fisher line merely because the same forename recurs.

By the early seventeenth century, people named Glasgow were established in:

* Glasgow and its immediate hinterland;
* Stevenston, Corsinkell and Kilwinning in Ayrshire;
* Hirmanscheillis and other parts of Lothian;
* Mid Calder and Kirknewton;
* Edinburgh and Leith;
* Stirling;
* and the Borders.

Some were probably offshoots of the Glasgow burgh families. Others may descend from separate late-medieval bearers. Several routes may be represented at once.

==== Marriage and civic association ====

The family’s marriages and recurring associates show how the surname became embedded within Lowland society.

Directly documented marriages include:

* [[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]] and [[Spreull-4|Jonet Spreull]];
* [[Glasgow-3522|William Glasgow]] and [[Herbison-439|Margaret Herbesoun]];
* [[Glasgow-1096|Robert Glasgow]] and [[Rolland-239|Margaret Rolland]];
* [[Glasgow-1097|Archibald Glasgow]] and [[Newlands-647|Isobell Newlands]];
* [[Glasgow-3188|Ninian Glasgow]] and [[Meik-14|Jonet Meik]];
* [[Glasgow-1027|Robert Glasgow]] and [[Cunningham-20923|Jonet Cunningham]].

These connections placed Glasgow households among families involved in burgh property, craft and merchant activity, clerical service, local administration and minor landholding.

The marriage of John Glasgow and Jonet Spreull provides a secure Glasgow–Spreull connection by 1534. It does not, by itself, establish Jonet’s exact place within the Spreulls of Cowden or Ladymuir.

Likewise, the Herbison, Hutcheson, Rolland, Newlands and Meik connections are valuable where they are supported by protocols and testaments. Their importance lies in reconstructing real legal and household networks rather than attaching each spouse to the most prominent family bearing the same surname.

Later appearances of Cunningham, Stewart, Hamilton, Graham, Scot, Fraser and other surnames may reflect widening social and geographical connections. They do not automatically prove marriage into senior noble or chiefly houses.

Each claimed relationship still requires documented parentage, an estate designation, a marriage contract, sasine, testament or equivalent contemporary evidence.

==== Overall picture ====

The evidence does not support either of two simple extremes:

* one fully proved dynasty descending from a single medieval John;
* or a set of entirely unrelated households sharing the surname by coincidence.

The more defensible picture is of a surname which had become fixed by the later fifteenth century and was carried into the sixteenth century by several people operating within overlapping urban and regional networks.

One burgh pedigree can presently be followed securely through William, John, Stephen and the younger William. Beside it stand the fisher family of Robert and Ninian, the Corsinkell family, the Hirmanscheillis household and other property-holding couples whose exact connections remain under investigation.

<blockquote>
'''The network is visible; the complete pedigree is not.'''
</blockquote>

Detailed profile assessments, source extracts, branch tables and unresolved relationships are available at:

'''[https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Space:Glasgow_Branches_in_15th_and_16th_Century_Scotland Early Glasgow Branches in Scotland, c.1447–1650]'''

=== 3. Religious conflict, Presbyterian settlement and Ulster migration, c.1650–1800 ===

The second half of the seventeenth century reshaped many Scottish families through religious conflict, political upheaval and migration.

The '''Covenanters''' were Scottish Presbyterians who opposed attempts by the Stuart monarchy to impose bishops and greater royal control over the Kirk. The movement began with the National Covenant of 1638 and helped drive the Bishops’ Wars and the wider Wars of the Three Kingdoms.

After the Restoration of Charles II in 1660, episcopacy was reimposed. Many nonconforming ministers and worshippers faced fines, imprisonment and transportation, particularly during the later seventeenth-century persecution remembered as the “Killing Time”.

Direct evidence of Glasgow involvement survives in the Borders. '''[[Glasgow-1498|John Glasgow]]''' and '''[[Glasgow-1605|William Glasgow]]''' of Cavers, Roxburghshire, were among the prisoners transported after the Battle of Bothwell Bridge who survived the 1679 wreck of the ''Croune of London''. Their story places at least one Borders family directly within the Covenanter experience.

The surname should not, however, be treated as uniformly Covenanter. The Cavers prisoners provide direct evidence for one group, while other Glasgow families remained integrated into local office, landed society and the Presbyterian settlement established after 1688–90.

The Ayrshire family belongs more clearly to the Presbyterian settlement which emerged at the end of this period.

'''[[Glasgow-1073|John Glasgow]]''' graduated M.A. at Glasgow in 1674 and was ordained minister of Kilbirnie on 16 August 1688, the same year in which his Episcopalian predecessor was removed. No surviving record yet identifies John himself as a field preacher, prisoner or active Covenanter. He is better described as a Presbyterian minister of the Revolution settlement.<ref name="FastiKilbirnie">Hew Scott, ''Fasti Ecclesiae Scoticanae'', vol. III (Edinburgh, 1920), pp. 102–103; [https://archive.org/details/fastiecclesiaesc03scot Internet Archive].</ref>

John married first '''[[Cunningham-20924|Jean Cunningham]]''', eldest daughter of John Cunningham of Wattieston, chamberlain to the laird of Kilbirnie, and secondly Margaret Scott.

His son '''[[Glasgow-1077|John Glasgow, M.A.]]''' later served as bailie and several times as provost. '''[[Glasgow-1075|Dr Robert Glasgow]]''' was a surgeon and chamberlain to Viscount Garnock. The line later produced '''[[Glasgow-1076|Sir Robert Glasgow of Mountgreenan]]'''.

Later Glasgow–Cunninghame couples include '''[[Glasgow-1227|Abraham Glasgow]]''' and '''[[Cunningham-20925|Janet Cunnyngham]]''' (married in 1741), '''[[Glasgow-1321|Alexander Glasgow]]''' and '''[[Cunningham-20926|Agnes Cunninghame]]''', and '''[[Glasgow-1483|James Glasgow]]''' and '''[[Cunningham-20927|Jean Cunninghame]]'''. The years 1719, 1747 and 1790 previously shown here were profile birth years, not marriage dates. These repeated pairings are useful research leads, but do not by themselves prove that the spouses belonged to one continuous Cunningham lineage or social network.

{{Image|file=Glasgow_Name_Study-1.jpg
|align=r
|size=m
|caption=Glasgow family memorials at Kilwinning Abbey
}}

The memorials at Kilwinning belong to this later Ayrshire setting. They demonstrate an established regional presence, although they do not by themselves prove descent from the medieval ''de Glasgu'' bearers or the sixteenth-century Glasgow burgh family.

During the same broad period, Glasgow households became established in Ulster.

The earliest proposed Antrim presence is '''[[Glasgow-1078|Robert Glasgow]]''', recorded in the county during the 1640s and later associated with Larne. By 1669, '''[[Glasgow-1081|James Glascho]]''' and John Glascho were separately recorded in Kilwaughter parish. Later families appear in Presbyterian congregational networks across Antrim, Tyrone and County Londonderry as farmers, tradesmen and church elders.

A later family tradition places '''[[Glasgow-591|William Glasgow]]''' among the Williamite forces connected with the relief of Derry before settlement in Tyrone. This remains a tradition pending contemporary military or settlement evidence.

The move to Ulster did not necessarily represent one migration or one family. Some households may have crossed for land and economic opportunity, while others moved through Presbyterian networks or under pressure from political and religious conflict.

The Antrim, Tyrone and Londonderry families should remain separate until tenancy, church, probate, migration or DNA evidence joins them.

These are working research groups, not four branches of one proved pedigree.

By the eighteenth century, the surname was established in both Scotland and Ulster. Scottish families remained visible in Ayrshire, Lothian and the Borders, while Ulster families developed their own Presbyterian, farming and trading networks before later migration overseas.

=== 4. Migration and worldwide families, c.1700 onward ===

From Scotland and Ulster, Glasgow families later moved into North America, the Caribbean, Australia, New Zealand and other parts of the British world.

These movements did not form one simple migration chain. Different households left at different periods and for different economic, religious, military and family reasons.

Some settled as farmers and tradesmen. Others became merchants, soldiers, ministers, physicians and public officials.

Notable examples include:

* [[Glasgow-634|James Glasgow]], North Carolina Secretary of State;
* [[Glasgow-1220|William Glasgow, later Glass]], founder of the permanent settlement on Tristan da Cunha;
* [[Glasgow-473|Ellen Glasgow]], Pulitzer Prize-winning novelist;
* [[Glasgow-773|Sir Thomas William Glasgow]], Australian general.

Passenger records, migrant profiles and overseas research are indexed at:

<span id='dna_research'></span>
== DNA research ==

The DNA project compares documented paternal lines and uses Y-DNA to identify genetic families, estimate shared ancestors and direct further documentary research.

Genetic estimates remain separate from named pedigrees unless records establish the connection.

A DNA match can support the conclusion that two tested male lines share a paternal ancestor. It cannot, by itself:

* identify that ancestor as a named medieval bearer;
* prove every parent-child attachment in an online tree;
* establish where the ancestor lived;
* or determine when the surname was first adopted.

The most useful tests are those attached to independently documented paternal pedigrees.

* [[Space:Glasgow Ancient YDNA|Ancient Y-DNA and deep ancestry]]

* [https://groups.io/g/glasgowdnaproject Glasgow DNA Project discussion group]
* [https://www.familytreedna.com/public/Glasgow FamilyTreeDNA Glasgow Project]

<span id='research_status'></span>
== Research status ==

'''Documented:'''

* personal use of ''de Glasgu'' from the late twelfth century;
* repeated pre-1400 use as an identifying second name;
* fixed or unprefixed surname forms by the later fifteenth century;
* documentary surname continuity into the sixteenth century;
* a proved burgh pedigree beginning with William Glasgow, Esbell Brade and their son John;
* separate sixteenth-century Glasgow families at Corsinkell and Hirmanscheillis;
* a fisher and burgess family centred on Robert and Ninian Glasgow;
* established Glasgow households in later Scottish and Ulster records;
* a principal tested Glasgow Y-DNA cluster sharing R-FT25406, alongside separately tracked genetic groups.

'''Principal questions:'''

* Did the medieval bearers belong to one family or several independent locative groups?
* Was the Glasgow burgess of 1447–1455 the Stirling witness of 1475–1479/80?
* Which late-medieval bearer, if any, was an ancestor of William Glasgow?
* Was the Robert Glasgow recorded as a fisher and citizen the father named in Ninian Glasgow’s 1596 burgess admission?
* How did the Corsinkell, Glasgow burgh, Lothian and Border families connect?
* Which Spreull, Hutcheson, Herbison, Cunningham, Stewart, Hamilton, Graham, Scot and Fraser spouses belonged to documented landed or cadet families?
* How do the principal Scottish and Ulster groups connect?
* Which documentary pedigrees correspond to the principal surname-era Y-DNA branches?

'''Research standard:'''

Documentary occurrence, personal identity, relationship and reconstructed lineage are recorded separately.

Shared surnames, locations, occupations, witnesses and naming patterns are useful clues. They are not proof of a specific relationship.

One Tree exports and connected WikiTree profiles are research maps rather than genealogical sources. Every parent-child link should ultimately rest on a contemporary or near-contemporary record, a reliable edited source or a clearly identified inferential argument.

== How to contribute ==

Useful additions include:

* original records or complete transcriptions;
* precise page, folio and archive references;
* wills, sasines, leases, rentals, marriage contracts and church records naming relatives;
* documented parentage for spouses in the principal marriage clusters;
* evidence connecting property across generations;
* documented male-line pedigrees for Y-DNA comparison;
* corrections to duplicate, conflated or chronologically impossible profiles;
* and evidence distinguishing people who shared the same forename and surname.

Researchers and descendants can join the [https://groups.io/g/glasgowdnaproject Glasgow DNA Project discussion group].

== Project governance ==

The Name Study is managed as an evidence-led research project rather than a single compiled pedigree.

{| class="wikitable sortable" style="padding:5px; width:100%;"
|+ '''Project standards'''
|-
! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | Area
! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | Standard
|-
| '''Documentary claims''' || Cite the original record image or official archive entry where available. Identify published abstracts, transcriptions and family histories as derivative sources.
|-
| '''Relationships''' || Record a parent, spouse or child as proved only when a source states the relationship or a transparent evidence argument excludes reasonable alternatives.
|-
| '''Uncertainty''' || Preserve uncertain people and locations while research continues. Do not detach or blank them unless evidence supports a specific replacement applied in the same edit.
|-
| '''Pre-1500 people''' || Maintain one individual free-space page per distinct bearer and link it from the chronological register; do not create a WikiTree person profile for this study.
|-
| '''DNA''' || Use Y-DNA to compare documented paternal pedigrees. Do not assign a modern SNP to a named historical person without a documentary male-line bridge or relevant ancient DNA.
|-
| '''Project workbench''' || Treat [https://glasgow.phenotype.dev/ Glasgow Surname Project] maps, matches and catalogue associations as finding aids; cite the underlying record on WikiTree.
|-
| '''Corrections''' || Explain the evidence, retain superseded sources where they remain identifiable, and record material identity or relationship conclusions in the affected profile research notes.
|}

'''Decision path:''' a proposed connection begins as a research lead, becomes a documented occurrence when its source is inspected, becomes an identity or relationship hypothesis when the records are compared, and becomes a project conclusion only when the evidence and alternatives are stated on the relevant hub.
